title: Resting in the Six Senses
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The teacher reflects on the recent losses of four Zen Center priests who embodied the principles of Zen practice, such as perseverance and humility, and sees these losses as an opportunity for new life to emerge. He encourages the community to continue growing and evolving through their practice, embracing impermanence and preciousness in all relationships. By letting go of attachment to expectations and judgments, we can cultivate a deeper connection with others and find happiness and joy in the present moment.

sentences.text: Good morning, everybody.
It's so nice to be here with everybody.
Welcome, Kate and Michael.
And Marilyn.
Hi, Marilyn.
I haven't seen you in a while.
How are you doing?
Well, I had a wild ride up here last night from Eugene, Oregon.
Oh my goodness.
Good heavens.
You can hardly see the road because there is so much water being [unclear: "fired off the tracks"].
Yes.
I was wondering yesterday, why is it always raining harder on the freeway than anywhere else?
Do you ever notice that?
It's really strange.
Well, I really appreciate that we're doing the oryoki meals in the zendo.
I hope it wasn't too hard on everybody.
I realize I sometimes try to think of how it must look through your eyes, and it might seem bizarre or overly obsessive, compulsive, Zen, hyper-ritualistic mania.
But to me it's just very touching, because this is how I ate all my meals when I was young.
When I was a young man, for many years, this is how I ate all my meals.
So even though you couldn't hear it, when Lise made the food offering this morning, I could hear the Buddha drum with a big crescendo when she lifted the offering up.
I know you couldn't hear it, but I could hear it.
It was very wonderful.
So I really appreciate it.
Thank you for indulging an old guy's youthful lunacy.
Thank you.
It is a great practice, and I hope that by the time we are finished with six meals or whatever it is, seven meals in three days, you will come to appreciate the beauty of this ritual.
It reminds me of all these years of practicing with people, and I'm sure many of you already can appreciate this: when you enter into this ritual space together, you create a bond between you.
It is unlike, I guess it's just friendship like any other friendship, and yet it somehow has a special quality to it.
I'm thinking of this because in the last few months, up until just the other day, we've lost four Zen Center priests that I practiced with all the years.
Four of them died just in the last several months.
So even though you don't know them, I'm just going to tell you about them a little bit, because they're on my mind.
I just found out yesterday that the fourth one passed away.
The first one who died was Jerome Peterson, who was one of the earliest students of Suzuki Roshi.
I think he was in his 80s, and he still lived in 300 Page Street as a monk, getting up every day, putting on his robe, going to the zendo.
He had many physical problems so he could barely walk, but he remained practicing every day, and bright.
Someone told me, I didn't know this, that Jerome used to have a little group that would read the Avatamsaka Sutra every week.
That's why I was thinking of it last night.
Every week, and it took him 18 years to get through.
It's a very long sutra.
When they came to the end, the last page after 18 years, he picked up the first page and just started over again.
Without saying anything, he just picked up the book and started over again.
He was an amazing guy, Jerome.
He had the worst zazen posture of anybody in history.
When you saw Jerome sitting in sesshin, you didn't know if there was a person there or if it was just a crumpled-up pile of robes.
You couldn't tell.
He was amazing.
When we were in Japan, Suzuki Roshi was talking about this, and he said it's called squashed persimmon posture.
There's a name for it there, squashed persimmon.
So we're all getting there, little by little.
Jerome was a remarkable person, and it's a great loss.
He was a fixture at San Francisco Zen Center forever and ever and ever.
Then Darlene Cohen died.
Darlene is known to many of you because she was a very powerful Zen teacher.
A very funny, lively person who, because of her rheumatoid arthritis, specialized in teachings that had to do with coping with strong pain.
She wrote many books that maybe now that she's gone will speak even more loudly than they did when she was alive.
There was a big funeral for her just the other day at Green Gulch, although she died a few months ago.
Not long after she died, Lou Hartman died.
Many of you know Blanche Hartman, who's a sewing teacher and former abbess of San Francisco Zen Center.
She and Lou were married for 63 years, I think.
Can you imagine?
He was in his 90s, and I always tell the story of Lou.
It's hard to believe, but it's true.
Lou never wanted to be a Zen teacher or any kind of Zen leader.
He was just completely uninterested in that.
But every now and then he would be asked to give a talk, and he would give a talk.
So it was a rare occasion when he would give a Dharma talk, maybe once every year or couple of years.
And he always gave the same talk.
Maybe I told you about this already, did I?
No?
He always gave the same talk.
He would walk into the zendo and he would say, "Well, I had a talk all prepared, but something happened to me as I was walking into the zendo, and I realized that I had to throw that entire talk out.
It's completely irrelevant, and everything that's happened to me so far in my life, completely gone.
I have to start all over again right now."

Then he would give the talk, and in the talk he would explain all the things that he had been through and that had failed him in his life, up to and including Zen Buddhism, which he just realized as he walked into the room had failed him.
And now he had nothing to go on, nothing to say, nothing to believe in.
He gave that talk, but every time he gave it, it seemed as if it was the first time.
You know what I mean?
It seemed like it genuinely had happened to him.
Either he didn't remember that he did it before or I don't know what it was, but every time he gave that talk it was completely believable.
Maybe it wasn't just as he walked in, it might have been yesterday or an hour ago, but he would always describe what had happened that made him feel that way.
So he was really remarkable.
I saw him a couple of days before he died, and then again the day he died, actually.
I got to sit with him for a while.
The circumstances of his death left him a little [unclear: "battle-brained"], but still cogent, and it was wonderful to see him thinking through.
He was deciding, shall I go down the path to death or shall I try to turn back?
He was thinking this through, and he decided that he would go.
And then just yesterday I found out that Wendy Matlow, who had been practicing with us at San Francisco Zen Center in the 70s and 80s, died.
A young person, to me young, I think still in her 50s.
She had had many hard, difficult things happen, and eventually died of cancer.
Anyway, it's sad.
From my perspective, it's not only these wonderful people that we'll miss, but also this generation of people.
These are all people who came and founded the Zen Center and were the early group of people who built it up.
So now they're dying off, we're dying off, and of course that's what happens.
That enables new life to come forth and express itself, and that's what's happening.
There are wonderful new students at the Zen Center with strong commitment to practice and with their own vision of how to carry it forward.
Each person's leaving the scene enables another person to come forward.
Then that person also leaves, someone else comes, and that's our life.
Each one of us is a conduit for life passing on.
It is really something to think of practicing with someone for 10, 20, 30, 40 years, side by side together.
Even when people part ways, like Wendy Matlow, whom I haven't seen in quite a number of years, her passing makes me sad because of the time that we spent together practicing.
So without being overly melodramatic about all this, I would say, why don't we all just take a look around the room and look at these people who are in this room with you now, and think about it.
Think about how precious we are to one another.
I certainly feel that preciousness, and it's wonderful and inspiring and sad to realize that we will all lose one another, and that's how it goes.

I was in the airport yesterday walking around, and I thought, if you're smart and it's a disaster, like the world is falling apart, you look around and you really appreciate everybody, even strangers, right?
That's how I was walking around the airport thinking, and it is a disaster.
We are in a disaster.
And look at all these lovely people that I'm depending on, and they're depending on me.
That's how it is.
It's very sad.
I'm sorry to bring it down.
It's too early in the morning for thinking about all this, but anyway, that's how it is.
So my subject for today is a Zen story, and the name of the story is "Miracles."
Here's the story.
*One day while Guishan was lying down, Yangshan came to see him.*
By the way, speaking of Guishan and Yangshan, Tim sent me a great link.
Thank you, Tim.
It's embarrassing, isn't it?
Yeah, it's terrible.

It's a link to a website that has the names of all the Zen ancestors, and if you click on it, a voice comes up and tells you how to pronounce it, thereby making it clear to you that for 40 years you've been mispronouncing them.
However, I do not think I have been mispronouncing Guishan and Yangshan.
Others I've been mispronouncing, but Guishan and Yangshan, actually, those are the correct pronunciations.
Which brings up the question: maybe we pronounce it differently than they pronounce it in China.
How come they get to say how Americans pronounce Chinese names?
But never mind about that.
Don't things get Americanized after a while?
Never mind.
*One day while Guishan was lying down, Yangshan came to see him, and Guishan turned away to face the wall.
And Yangshan said, "I am your student.
Please don't be formal."
Guishan started to get up.
Yangshan rose to leave.
And Guishan said, "Yangshan," and Yangshan came back.
Guishan said, "Let me tell you about my dream."
Yangshan leaned forward to listen to Guishan's dream.
And Guishan said, "Would you interpret my dream for me?
I want to see how you do it."
So Yangshan brought a basin of water and a towel, and Guishan washed his face and sat up.
Then Xiangyan came in, and Guishan said, "Yangshan and I have been sharing miracles.
This is no small matter."
And Xiangyan said, "I was next door and I heard you."
Guishan said, "Why don't you try now?"
And Xiangyan made a bowl of tea and brought it to him.
Guishan praised them both, saying, "You two students surpass even Shariputra and Modgalyayana with your miraculous activity."*
That's the story.
It's a wonderful story about what I was talking about, about our beautiful Dharma relations and about our miraculous life.
They say about the Buddha that he had many miraculous powers and that his body had miraculous marks.
According to the sutras, there are 32 major and 80 minor marks of the Buddha's body, which are reflections of his inner condition and spiritual accomplishments.
You can find these listed in the various sutras.
They express the fact that the Buddha is no ordinary person.
He's nothing like you or me.
For instance, the Buddha's feet are perfectly level and smooth, like the breast of a tortoise.
Our feet are not flat and smooth, and they may be rough on the bottom.
You ever feel the bottom of a tortoise's belly?
Very smooth.
So the Buddha has feet like that.
Also, the Buddha's feet and hands are inscribed with the impression of a thousand-spoked wheel.
There are little tattoos on his feet and hands, a thousand-spoked wheel.
And the fingers and toes of the Buddha's hands and feet are webbed.
You probably didn't know that, did you?
Webbed hands and feet like a duck.
But the webbing is not flesh.
It's light, brilliant light.
The Buddha is seven cubits tall, compared to ordinary people who never exceed four cubits, even very tall people, basketball players: four cubits.
But the Buddha is seven cubits tall.

The Buddha's fingers, toes, and arms are also extremely long, and there are places on the Buddha's body, among them his shoulders, his torso, his hands, feet, and the back of his neck, that are smooth and slightly raised.
The Buddha's skin is not like ours.
It's luminous and golden.
And his teeth are extremely white.
These are a few of the 32 marks of a Buddha.
In Zen, they say that the Buddha has six miraculous powers.

These are pretty different from the other lists of miraculous powers, which usually have things on them like clairvoyance, clairaudience, and the ability to be in several places in space in the same moment.
Those are the [unclear: "matched powers"] in other traditions of Buddhism that are listed.
But in Zen, there are six miraculous powers that are different from these.
In Zen, the six miraculous powers of a Buddha are the Buddha's miraculous ability to live completely within, and yet unencumbered by, the six sense organs, which includes thinking and feeling.
Those are the six miraculous powers, according to Zen.
In a way, these six miraculous powers seem so much more modest than the others, which seem so amazing.
These seem less amazing.
But Dogen comments and says that the other miraculous powers are actually minor powers, and the six miraculous powers of Zen are the major powers.
The minor powers, he says, are minor because they're rare.
They're limited to certain beings under certain conditions.
That's why they're minor.
But the six powers of the Buddha, according to Zen, are major miraculous powers because they are not limited to certain people or certain conditions.
Buddhas universally manifest these miraculous powers all the time, everywhere.
So what does all this mean?

It means exactly that it is miraculous to be alive, to be a living being, to breathe, to be able to sit peacefully, to be able to see, to be able to hear, to be able to smell, taste, touch, think, and feel emotions.
Of course this is miraculous.
I mean, isn't this miraculous?
Of course it is.
It's so obvious.
If these things didn't exist and somebody said, would you produce these things?
You couldn't even imagine them, let alone produce them.

And if we could see and hear and smell and taste and touch and think and feel with full appreciation, without being caught and spun around by our experience, we would experience and feel, literally, that this is so: that it is absolutely miraculous to function as a human being.
This is what the Zen masters mean when they talk about miracles.
What magician, what mystical genius could top this miracle?

*To be a living, functioning, conscious human being.* Dogen says, *"The entire world of Ten Directions is the true body of a single monk."* Once Linji described all these spectacular superpowers that Buddhas and other sorcerers have.
And he said, *"The miracles I've just described are the result of past actions or present situations.
But the six types of miracles of a Buddha are different.
A Buddha enters forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touchables, an object of mind, and is not confused by them, is not caught by them.
Thus a Buddha masters the six sense objects, which are all marked with emptiness.
And a Buddha is free of conditions.
Even having a body of five skandhas, accompanied by desire, a Buddha does not depend on anything.
A Buddha practices miracles that are grounded on the earth."*
So, getting back to our story.
One day, Guishan was lying down, and Yangshan came to see him, and Guishan turned to face the wall.
Yangshan said, "I am your student, please don't be formal."
I wonder why Guishan turns to face the wall when Yangshan comes in.
Maybe this is ordinary human relations, in which, although we don't necessarily think of this or know this, there's always a degree of formality.
There's always a degree of distance and pretense.
When we greet another person, we always turn away at first.
It seems most polite to do so.
Let's not overwhelm one another with our miraculous presence, with the full force of our miraculous presence.
It's much better to be nice and to be polite, and let the other person have time to adjust to us and get comfortable.
And we do this.
Yangshan says to Guishan, "No, please teacher, there's no need to be formal with me.
I am ready to receive your presence."
And this happens in our lives too.

Especially, as I was saying in the beginning, in our Dharma relations, people indicate to us one way or another, often without words, and often without even knowing that they're doing so, that they are ready and willing to receive our presence.
And then if we are willing to, as in our story Guishan is willing, we accommodate the other person, we share our presence.
This is actually rare and wonderful when it happens.
Guishan started to get up, Yangshan rose to leave.
It's interesting what happens next in the story.
Guishan gets up, Yangshan gets ready to leave.
They're so sweet to each other, so respectful, so sensitive to one another.
They don't want to disturb one another.
And this is the greatest courtesy of all, don't you think?
The courtesy to leave each other alone.
This is the greatest respect for oneself, to leave oneself alone, for you to leave the other alone.

This is great, not to make a fuss, not to make a judgment or an evaluation or an improvement, not to meddle, but to completely generously open up the widest possible space for whatever needs to unfold without knowing what it is.
Guishan called out Yangshan and Yangshan came back.
Guishan said, "Let me tell you about my dream."
And Yangshan leaned forward to listen, and that's when Guishan said, "Would you interpret my dream for me?
I want to see how you do it."
And Yangshan brings a basin of water and a towel.
Guishan washes his face and sits up.
This is something, a trope, so to speak, that you see all the time in Zen stories, where somebody calls and somebody else responds.
When you call someone, they answer.
When someone calls your name, you say yes.
You don't think about it, you just do it.
And this is another miracle, that we call out to one another and that we respond to one another.
It's a bad feeling if you call somebody repeatedly and they never respond.
Doesn't it feel bad?
When they do respond, it's wonderful.
You feel alive because the other person has responded to you.
And the person responds without thinking it over, without scheming.
We all do this.
We all respond when we're called.
And this must be a kind of imitation of early Buddhist sutras, which often would begin, they would always begin, "Thus have I heard, the Buddha was at such and such a place," and so on and so on.
And then often the Buddha would begin by saying, "O monastics."
And they would say, "Yes, Buddha."
And then he would begin to give the teaching.
I guess he was checking to see if they were really there and really ready to listen.
And the Zen masters must have read these early sutras and thought about them and said, well, if someone is really there and calls out and someone responds, you don't need anything else.
That's all you need.
You don't need any details.
That's the only teaching we ever need.
So seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, thinking, feeling are Buddha miracles.
How much more so?
Because if we had all of that but didn't know how to respond and call each other, we would not have this human world.
So that's another miracle.
Calling and responding.
The willingness that each and every one of us has evidenced in our lives to be a person among people.
The willingness to be called and to call others and to respond.
So that's the second miracle of our story.
So Guishan says, "I want to tell you about my dream.
Will you interpret it for me?"
What dream does he mean?
He doesn't tell him any dream.
It's this dream, this deeply mysterious, deeply unconscious enactment that we call everyday life.
Believe me, everyday life is not what it seems to be.
It really is a dream.
So much is going on that we don't know.
So just the way the major miracle isn't webbed fingers and toes and a golden body.
In a way that's easy.
The major miracle is life.
So also the real dream is not monsters under the bed and lurid imagery.
The real dream is this one right now.
The dream in which I'm talking and you're listening and we're sitting here together.
What a beautiful dream.
And Guishan and Yangshan are in the same dream.
They don't even need to talk about it.
And it's not a matter of words and concepts and explanations.
Guishan just woke up and usually when you wake up, you want to wash your face.
So Yangshan brings him a basin and a towel.
He doesn't think he's doing something really good.
He just brings him a basin because that's what anyone would do in a dream of waking up from a dream.
So Xiangyan comes in and Guishan says, "Yangshan and I have been sharing miracles.
This is no small matter."
Xiangyan said, "I was next door and heard you."
Guishan said, "Why don't you try now?"
And Xiangyan made a bowl of tea and brought it to him.
And that's when Guishan praises them.
"You two students surpass even Shariputra and Maudgalyayana with your miraculous activity.
It is no small matter to live together in harmony, sharing one understanding about life."
This is the greatest thing, to live and die together like this, with mutual understanding.
What a miracle.
So it seems we have miracles piled on top of miracles.
We have seeing, hearing, tasting, touching, thinking, feeling without being entangled, but in freedom to receive a world.
That's a miracle.
And responding as a person when we're called forth by others and calling forth others.
That's a miracle.
And our being willing to let go and just live together with intimacy and understanding beyond personality, beyond social custom, beyond what we need and provide for one another.
This is a human possibility.
We all understand that it's possible.
This is a human miracle.
This miracle of love and friendship and mutual concern.
I use the word love, but notice that the word love is not used in this story.
The word compassion is not used in this story.
Because the kind of connection that's being described here is really beyond those words.
It's much more than this.
When we say love and compassion, it implies another outside oneself to be compassionate toward.
But there is no such one.
Guishan is Guishan, and Yangshan is Yangshan, and Xiangyan is Xiangyan.
And also they are the Buddha and Shariputra and Maudgalyayana.
Their lives, as ours, are archetypes of deeply connected, miraculous human sharing.
Compassion is too small a word for this.
Miracles.
There are only miracles.
Miraculous appearances that dance together for a while in order to enact together a beautiful dream.
One dream without boundaries.
So here's another story about miracles.
Yangshan was once attending on Yunyan, and Yunyan said to him, "Dongshan, what are miracles?"
Dongshan politely brought his hands together at his chest, and stood near him saying nothing.
Yunyan again asked, "What are miracles?"
Dongshan said goodbye and left.
So Dongshan is our great Chinese ancestor who is one of the two names that go in to make up the Japanese reading of Soto.
Dongshan in Japanese is Tozan, the toe of Soto.
And I always appreciated his story.
Yunyan was his teacher, but they didn't spend that much time together.
Dongshan actually studied more with other people, even though Yunyan was his root teacher.
We were in [unclear: "Luna Lake"] in November.
We were talking about Dongshan's great teaching of the insentient beings preaching the Dharma.
He said about his teacher, "I really appreciate you because you never taught me anything."
Somehow, without teaching anything, they had a wordless understanding together.
So this story is an image of perfect accord between teacher and disciple.
Usually the disciple asks the teacher a question, but here it's the teacher asking the disciple a question.
And I don't think it's in the spirit of testing or probing the disciple.
I think it's a genuine, serious, open-ended question.
What are miracles?
We've been saying that it's a miraculous power of seeing, hearing, feeling, thinking, tasting, touching, and so on, without being caught.
Easy to say, but actually it's quite hard not being caught by our acts of perception, thought, and emotion, because we have desire and we have grasping.
And we're getting caught all the time.
Maybe we can't prevent this.
So how can we be not caught even when we're caught, so that we don't add pain on top of pain and squirm around blindly, flailing our arms and legs and making even more trouble?
Which is what we do, right?
That's what human beings do.
How not to do that?
How do we open up the hand of thought in all our acts of thinking, feeling, and perception in this human world?
How do we do that?
This is really an open question that we have to keep asking, and we find ourselves, time and time again, caught.
So we have to keep asking.
We have to remind ourselves of this all the time.
We will never stop asking these questions and we will never stop making these efforts.
And here, the great teacher, Yunyan, still has this question.
And who better to ask the question to than one's own disciple?
He doesn't need to go around finding a higher class teacher than him.
He only needs to ask his disciple.
And Dongshan's answer is so beautiful.
He simply bows with respect and remains.
He stays forever in relation to his teacher.
That's how he helps him.
And then, when the question persists, he says goodbye and he withdraws.
Leaving is one of the most profound ways of remaining together forever.
The Buddha said all meeting ends in parting.
We couldn't meet if we didn't part.
That's how come we meet.
That's what enables us to meet, is that we will part.
Meeting and parting is one human gesture.
Sorrow and love always mingle.
That's the truth of our life and that's the deepest miracle of all.
So Dongshan expresses this by leaving.
And that's how he helps out his teacher.
So one last short story.
Long ago there was a sorcerer who had five miraculous powers and he visited the Buddha.
And he said, "You have six miraculous powers and I have five.
So which one am I missing?"
And the Buddha called to him, "Sorcerer?"
"Yes," he responded.
And the Buddha said, "Which miraculous power are you asking about?"
So this is a funny story.
Probably the sorcerer had amazing powers.
The story doesn't tell you what they were, but I'm sure he could fly through space and do all kinds of things, turn himself into other kinds of figures.
And the Buddha's powers, as we've been saying, are much less spectacular than that.
I bet you the Buddha couldn't pull a rabbit out of a hat or saw a person in half, like the sorcerer probably could.
And maybe the Buddha couldn't even fly or be in several places at once.
All the Buddha could do is eat his meal and go to the toilet and call out to someone, like the sorcerer, with measured kindness.
That's the only thing the Buddha could do.
The sorcerer, who actually had powers, wonders which power he's missing.
The Buddha, who has no other power than the power of being fully alive and knowing what his life actually is, doesn't think he has any miraculous powers.
Which power is the sorcerer missing?
Notice what happens in this story.
And I'm telling this story for Edie.
It's a special thing to realize for your ceremony on Sunday.
This is the secret to the ceremony.
Notice that the Buddha is not caught by the question.
Sometimes questions catch us, and as soon as we accept the question on its own terms, we're already caught and there's no way out.
This does not happen to the Buddha.
He doesn't get stuck in the question.
And this is an instruction for us, too, all the time.
Can we not get stuck in what happens?
Can we just let what happens happen and then call out and respond and not get stuck in the past?
The past exists, and it has its power.
I'm not saying it doesn't.
But can we respect that power and not get caught?
And the Buddha does not get caught.
He just calls out with kindness to the sorcerer.
And the sorcerer, lo and behold, responds.
And this is the Buddha's miraculous power in action.
And the sorcerer's miraculous power in action.
Because also the sorcerer is alive.
The sorcerer has human subjectivity and identity.
Maybe in that moment he sets aside his spectacular powers and joins the Buddha in the Buddha's miraculous powers.
So what power is missing in the sorcerer?
What power is missing in us?
Put in mind, realizing how precious and wonderful is this short time we have together in this wonderful Dharma hall.

I was just walking outside and seeing the new, I think they're new, boxes outside for growing things and the beautiful sign and the beautiful building and everything that's gone into making this place that receives us.
Can we appreciate the miracles that are here on each occasion when we're caught?
Can we know we're caught and let go?
Can we find some happiness?
Not later, but now.
Some joy right now in this precious gift of practicing together, this miraculous gift of practicing together.
So thank you all for being here and for listening to my talk.
Please take care.

verbatim.text: Good morning everybody. It's so nice to be here with everybody. Welcome Kate and Michael. And Marilyn. Hi Marilyn. I haven't seen you in a while. How are you doing? How are you doing? Well, I had a wild ride up here last night from Eugene, Oregon. Oh my goodness. Good heavens. Good heavens. You can hardly see the road because there is so much water being fired off the tracks. Yes. Yes, I was wondering yesterday, why is it always raining harder on the freeway than anywhere else? Do you ever notice that? It's really strange. Well, I really appreciate that we're doing the oryoki meals in the zendo. I hope it wasn't too hard on everybody.

I realize I sometimes try to think of it how it must look through your eyes and it might seem bizarre or overly obsessive, compulsive, zen, hyper ritualistic mania. But to me it's just very touching because this is how I ate all my meals when I was young. When I was a young man for many years, this is how I ate all my meals. And so even though you couldn't hear it, when Lise made the food offering this morning, I could hear the Buddha drum with a big crescendo when she lifted the offering up. I know you couldn't hear it, but I could hear it. It was very wonderful. So I really appreciate it. Thank you for indulging an old guy's youthful lunacy. Thank you. And it is a great practice and I hope that by the time we are finished with six meals or whatever it is, seven meals in three days, you will come to appreciate the beauty of this ritual. But it reminds me of all these years of practicing with people and I'm sure many of you already can appreciate this, that when you enter into this ritual space together, you create a bond between you.
